Iran hasn’t tried to repair nuclear facilities damaged in US strikes, UN nuclear chief says
articles.description: Iran hasn’t tried to repair nuclear facilities damaged in US strikes, UN nuclear chief says AP News Nuclear Inspectors See No Evidence Iran Fixed Bombed Sites Bloomberg.com Security Council, 10253rd Meeting (AM) Iran/Non-proliferation UN Meetings Coverage and Press Releases Director General Statement to the United Nations Security Council International Atomic Energy Agency UN Nuclear Watchdog Chief Urges Iran To Gran
articles.content: UNITED NATIONS (AP) — The head of the U.N. nuclear agency said Tuesday there has been no indication Iran has tried to repair or reconstruct its nuclear facilities damaged in U.S. and Israeli military strikes this year or last year. President Donald Trump has said one of the major reasons the U.S. went to war with Iran on Feb. 28 was to deny Tehran the ability to develop nuclear weapons, even as he has insisted that strikes the U.S. carried out on Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025 “obliterated” the country’s atomic program. During a U.N. Security Council meeting, International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi urged Iran to give inspectors access to all nuclear sites, including those damaged in the military attacks. The IAEA has not been able to verify the status of Iran’s stockpile of near weapons-grade uranium since the U.S. bombed its sites last year. However, Grossi said that “since June 2025, we have not identified any activity to repair or reconstruct any of the facilities damaged in the military attacks of 2025 and 2026.” Trump has consistently downplayed the economic impact of the Iran war, which has emerged as a liability for Republicans heading into next week’s midterm elections, and has argued that higher fuel prices are worth paying to prevent a nuclear-armed Iran. The White House didn’t immediately respond Tuesday evening to a request for comment on Grossi’s remarks. Iran maintains that its nuclear program is peaceful. However, the IAEA says the country has a stockpile of 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60% purity — a short, technical step away from weapons-grade levels of 90%. The U.N. meeting on Tuesday was called by Bahrain, Denmark, Latvia, France, the United Kingdom and United States after the IAEA referred Iran to the Security Council for failing to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations. Russia and China, allies of Iran, tried unsuccessfully to prevent the meeting. Under those obligations, which are part of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, Iran is legally bound to declare all nuclear material and activities and allow IAEA inspectors to verify that none of it is being diverted from peaceful uses. Iran’s U.N. deputy ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi attacked the council for its silence after the U.S.-Israeli attacks, denouncing their “wars of aggression against Iran” and accusing the U.S. of committing war crimes against the Iranian people. He never mentioned the IAEA’s unanswered questions or the demand to return its inspectors. Instead, he asserted that “Israel possesses nuclear weapons, yet your concern is the absence of inspectors in Iran.” Israel has never confirmed that it possesses nuclear weapons. U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz called Iran a “brutal dictatorship” and asked if the Iranian ambassador wanted to apologize to Bahrain’s envoy, a council member, for attacking his country. “We’ve heard tireless allegations against the United States, ” he said. “What we have not heard today is an explanation for Iran’s continued failure to satisfy its safeguard obligations.” The IAEA asked Iran for answers, Waltz said, and it would be smart for the Iranian representative to start providing some answers.

Who should be believed? Trump's social media post on golf course leads lawyers back to court
articles.description: Who should be believed? Trump's social media post on golf course leads lawyers back to court AP News Hours after a federal judge put his golf course project on hold, President Trump said he’s closing East Potomac on November 15 anyway WUSA9 Judge demands Trump lawyers answer the big question: Is the president lying? The Independent Judge Temporarily Blocks Further Alterations at D.C.’s East Potomac Park The New York
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — Donald Trump’s social media posts on the renovation of a historic golf course in the nation’s capital are putting Justice Department lawyers in the uncomfortable position of explaining whether the president of the United States should be believed or not. U.S. Judge Ana Reyes said Tuesday that the department should clarify “whether any plan exists to close East Potomac Golf Course on or around November 15, 2026.” She ordered Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. to appear in court Friday or Monday for a status hearing. Tuesday’s order came in response to Trump’s social media post late Monday criticizing Reyes’ temporary injunction stopping work at East Potomac Park. That injunction, issued Monday, was in large part due to previous Trump announcements — via social media — that plans had been completed for the golf course and construction would begin next month. Trump said the facility would be closed for 15 months. The following day he set the timetable to “immediately.” Reyes said: “Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting president. Not to believe him that a cabinet secretary has ‘developed’ a federal land project. Not to believe him that the secretary’s agency will destroy a historic golf course already on the land. Not to believe him that ‘restoration work’ will begin ’IMMEDIATELY!’ Not to believe him that the course ‘will be closed’ for over a year. Not to believe what the president has repeatedly told the American public.” The current preliminary injunction temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the East Potomac Golf Course. The administration must give 10 days’ notice in writing before making any “irreparable modification” to any “forms or features” of the course while the lawsuit is active. The plaintiffs challenging the project, DC Preservation League and two golfers, claim the work is inflicting irreversible damage. Critics say Trump’s plan will make playing there unaffordable for the general public and destroy the site’s other uses. At one hearing, the judge excoriated the government after workers cut down at least 400 trees over a holiday weekend with little notice to the plaintiffs. A follow-up hearing Oct. 19 led to stunning exchanges, with Woodward at one point protecting a Justice Department lawyer during questioning when Reyes asked whom she should believe. “It’s difficult to put my colleague, a non-Senate-confirmed DOJ employee, in a position of contradicting the president,” Woodward said. The course renovation project is part of Trump’s aggressive campaign to leave his personal imprint on Washington’s historic landscape. Those plans include construction of a huge ballroom at the White House, a massive arch, and the creation of a National Garden of American Heroes in West Potomac Park. The DC Preservation League is part of a coalition of organizations, including the Cultural Landscape Foundation and one D.C. resident, who have filed lawsuits challenging those plans. There are several cases where judges have taken actions and issued injunctions or restraining orders because of the Trump administration’s push to begin work despite the pending lawsuits. The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The government filed a notice that it planned to appeal the temporary injunction with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.

articles.title: Pope says ‘there is no such thing as a holy war’ in message to religious leaders
articles.description: Pope says ‘there is no such thing as a holy war’ in message to religious leaders AP News Pope to Assisi Peace Meeting: 'May we be unarmed instruments of God's peace' Vatican News ‘There is no such thing as a holy war’: Pope Leo marks 40 years of Assisi peace meeting EWTN News The 'Spirit of Assisi' at 40 National Catholic Reporter Pope Leo to interfaith peace meeting: ‘War can never be waged in the name of God.’ Amer
articles.content: ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV on Tuesday denounced any religious justification for wars raging around the world, saying “there is no such thing as a holy war.” “Only peace is holy,” Leo said in a video-message to a gathering of religious leaders in the Italian hilltop town of Assisi. The American pope was supposed to have presided over the gathering in person, but had to cancel his participation as he recovers from Oct. 13 lung cancer surgery. Instead, Leo sent a videotaped message that was broadcast to the delegates, who included the Archbishop of Canterbury Sarah Mullally, spiritual leader of the worldwide Anglican Communion, as well as Muslim, Buddhist and other Christian leaders. They were in Assisi, the birthplace of the peace-loving St. Francis, to mark the 40th anniversary of a landmark interfaith peace meeting called by St. John Paul II. That encounter, controversial at the time because it featured leaders of different faiths praying together, spawned a movement of interreligious peace appeals and gatherings. In his message, the American pope denounced the “troubling revival of war as an instrument of international politics” and its religious justifications by leaders. “Precisely in these times marked by a culture of power, there is a need to cultivate the spirit of Assisi,” he said. “War can never be waged in the name of God,” he said. “We must rebuild peace everywhere, not prepare for more wars.” Russia’s Orthodox Church has justified Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as a “holy war” against a Western world it considers has fallen into evil. Leaders on all sides of the Iran war have used religion to justify their actions. U.S. officials, especially Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, have invoked their Christian faith to cast the war as a Christian nation trying to vanquish its foes with military might. Leo has consistently rejected such justifications as a perversion of religion itself, most stridently in his first encyclical “Magnificent Humanity” in which he said fighting in the name of religion “means attacking religion itself.” The Assisi gathering came as the Vatican is accelerating its humanitarian efforts for Ukraine following the entry into effect of a localized cease-fire in the devastated southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky. The pope’s chief almsgiver, Monsignor Luis Marín de San Martín, on Tuesday began a three-day visit to Ukraine and was bringing several trucks worth of winter clothes, blankets and food to Kyiv for distribution. Marín de San Martín was planning to visit Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro and Fastiv, Vatican News said. Leo had called for a cease-fire and the delivery of food and medicine in Oleshky, and the safe and voluntary evacuation of its people during an Oct. 16 phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, which the pontiff initiated from the hospital where he was recovering from surgery. Leo followed up three days later, back at the Vatican, with a call to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. According to the Vatican, Leo noted his appeal for a cease-fire to Putin and “expressed the hope that cooperation between both parties will allow for the delivery of food and medical aid, and for the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population.” The White House said the cease-fire in Oleshky was secured by first lady Melania Trump. Asked Tuesday, the Vatican foreign minister, Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, said the Vatican wasn’t aware of the first lady’s role but also dismissed any polemics over who was ultimately responsible. “I think it’s one of those situations in which it doesn’t matter who actually brought it about or who takes the credit, it’s the fact that hopefully it is real, it will last, it will allow for evacuation and it will allow the arrival of humanitarian aid to help the people who are left behind.” The Vatican initiatives took place after Italian Cardinal Matteo Zuppi, the papal envoy for the Ukraine-Russia war, finished his third mission to Moscow on Sept. 30 and the first under Leo’s pontificate. Zuppi has focused his initiatives on humanitarian issues, especially reuniting Ukrainian children taken by Russia with their families, and Gallagher said for now neither Russia nor Ukraine wants the Holy See to take on a greater mediation or facilitation role. US officials want Section 702 renewed before damaging court ruling goes public
articles.description: Senators say officials hid a ruling on warrantless searches past its release deadline.
articles.content: Senators say officials hid a ruling on warrantless searches past its release deadline. Two Democratic senators who have long overseen US intelligence say the Trump administration is illegally withholding a secret court’s findings from Congress until lawmakers renew a program that lets federal agents read Americans’ communications without a warrant. Seven months ago, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court objected to search filters that let intelligence analysts pull Americans’ messages from intercepted data without the approvals, written justifications, or records the law requires. The court approved another year of surveillance anyway. The ruling has never been made public, and Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Adam Schiff of California say the administration’s own deadline for releasing it passed in September. The program, Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), lapsed in June after Congress failed to renew it, though collection continues under the court’s March approval. The administration’s own public documentation says rulings like this one are reviewed for public release “within 180 days of issuance.” That window closed September 13, even as intelligence officials press lawmakers to reauthorize the program by the end of the year. Wyden, the longest-serving member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and Schiff, the former chair of its House counterpart, say the administration owes Congress an explanation for the delay, and the names of the officials responsible, by November 6. “If this administration won’t follow this simple statutory directive,” the senators told Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Attorney General Todd Blanche in a demand letter obtained exclusively by WIRED, “it is unclear why Congress or the American people should trust this administration to follow any of the other legal limits to Section 702.” Outside Congress, Demand Progress and 22 other civil liberties and government accountability groups on Monday urged congressional leaders to refuse to reauthorize Section 702 “while the administration actively withholds legally mandated information about how the surveillance program operates.” Signatories range from the American Civil Liberties Union to the conservative-backed Project for Privacy and Surveillance Accountability. The Trump administration has already been pressed, and has promised, to release the ruling. In April, Senators Tom Cotton and Mark Warner, the Intelligence Committee’s Republican chair and Democratic vice chair, pressed the administration to release it within 15 days so it could inform the Senate’s debate. In July, asked in writing whether he would commit to declassifying it by the 180-day deadline, Blanche replied, “Yes.” Warner “has been clear that he supports transparency with regard to Section 702,” his communications director, Rachel Cohen, tells WIRED. Neither former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard nor Bill Pulte, who briefly replaced her as acting director, “were responsive,” Cohen says, “but Senator Warner expects that DNI Clayton will declassify the opinion, consistent with the bipartisan letter and as required by law.” Cotton’s office did not respond to a request for comment. The White House, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and the US Justice Department did not answer questions WIRED sent Friday about the delay. Clayton, who is legally responsible as director of national intelligence for declassifying the ruling, has made no such promise. Asked before his July confirmation whether he would ensure the opinion was public before Congress voted on reauthorization, he wrote only that the government was “working arduously to expeditiously declassify” it and had made the full opinion available to lawmakers. Some of what the court found is already known. A FISA court opinion declassified last year described a similar FBI tool, a “participants filter” that let agents select people in contact with surveillance targets and read their messages. In February 2025, the Justice Department’s National Security Division told the court the tool had been running searches no one counted. The FBI shut it off the next month and switched it back on later that year, after the department approved a rebuilt version. This year’s ruling went beyond that. The court found that tools agencies use to narrow intercepted data to an American’s messages amount to searches of Americans, subject to the same limits, and ordered them rebuilt, The New York Times reported in April, citing unclassified administration talking points sent to lawmakers. Senator Alex Padilla said in a written question to Blanche that the Justice Department “is appealing portions” of the ruling “limiting the government’s use of certain filtering tools.” While the ruling stayed secret, seven intelligence agency fact sheets from March 2026, one dated the day of the ruling, cited a 98.9 percent compliance rate for FBI searches of Americans and credited Section 702 with stopping a planned terrorist attack on a Taylor Swift concert in Vienna. None mentions the court’s findings. The figure appears nowhere in the Justice Department inspector general’s October 2025 review of those searches, which put the compliance rate at 98.6 percent and could not conclude that “the FBI’s querying compliance issues are entirely in the past.” According to the fact sheets, FBI auditors review every such search. FBI Director Kash Patel closed the bureau’s Office of Internal Auditing last May and moved its auditors into another division. The bureau’s search counts before 2025 also omit queries run through the participants filter, searches the government’s own privacy watchdog says are “not possible to track.” Lawmakers who have read the ruling hint that it says more. Senator Dick Durbin, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, urged colleagues on the Senate floor in June to read it in a secure room. “I have seen it,” he said. Once they did, he told them, “your opinion of the role of FISA and the rights of Americans will be impacted for sure.” Wyden has also warned about a classified interpretation of Section 702 that he says multiple administrations have relied on and refused to declassify. “When it is eventually declassified,” he said in March, “the American people are going to be stunned that it took so long and that Congress had been debating this authority with insufficient information.” The Trump administration has until November 6 to answer the senators. The court’s current approval of the program expires in March. Surveillance reform advocates say the administration may try to avoid that fight by attaching a renewal to the annual defense authorization bill, which Congress usually finalizes in December. In 2023, lawmakers extended Section 702 for four months through that year’s defense bill after a Senate effort to strip the provision failed. This year’s House and Senate versions of the bill do not yet include it. This story originally appeared on wired.com.

articles.title: Detroit school district proposes bringing libraries back to 89 schools
articles.description: Detroit officials are proposing $251 million in projects, including expanded air conditioning and long-sought building upgrades. The plan could bring school libraries back by fall 2027.
articles.content: Sign up for Chalkbeat Detroit’s free newsletter to keep up with the city’s public school system and Michigan education policy. The Detroit district expects to have around $258.5 million in funding that may be used to fund long-sought school upgrades starting next year. Bringing libraries back to 89 schools is among the proposals the Detroit Public Schools Community District board is considering. If the board approves the plan in the coming months, the libraries could be partially open by fall 2027, Superintendent Nikolai Vitti said. During a board study session on Oct. 21, Vitti proposed spending $8.7 million in one-time funding to establish a library system. The money would cover the cost of up to 4,000 books per school, furniture, displays, initial staffing, and a new cataloging system. If adopted, the plan would reverse years of school library closures in the district tied to budget restraints and declining enrollment. Teachers in the district say many former library spaces are dormant or have been repurposed, leaving most students unable to access libraries during the school day. Vitti said staffing the libraries for three periods a day would cost about $5 million annually after the initial setup. LaTrice McClendon, chair of the board, said during the meeting that bringing school libraries back would be a significant step for the district. “I just want … to point out how historic this moment is,” McClendon said. The board has not yet voted on the district’s proposals for the one-time funding but is expected to do so at its November or December meeting. Many parents, educators, and community members have called on the district to restore school libraries as part of its efforts to improve students’ literacy proficiency. The same call has come from Michigan lawmakers, who have introduced bills to put libraries in nearly every Michigan public school in the state. None have passed. Michigan was below the national average for public schools with library media centers in the 2020-21 school year, according to the most recently available data from the National Center for Education Statistics. Only 74.6% of Michigan public schools had library media centers, compared with 87.6% nationally. Though many Detroit district schools have classroom libraries, there were only two certified librarians in the district in 2020. The district also lacks a library cataloging system. On Oct. 21, Vitti said if the board approves the proposal, the long-term plan would be to create a pathway for teachers to become certified school librarians. The certification process could be phased in over time, he added. “But in the short term, at least all the schools have libraries that are open for certain periods of the day, and not only certain periods of the day, but after school as well,” Vitti said. In the meantime, Vitti said the district would need to negotiate with the teachers union to potentially allow academic interventionists to run the libraries during part of their workday. The district’s proposal totaled $251 million and includes a range of building improvements and other projects, many of which have been called for by parents, staff, and community members for years. The $258.5 million will become available from several sources, according to district administrators. Vitti said Oct. 21 that the early learning centers are no longer needed because existing district buildings still have available pre-K seats. The original plan was made before Gov. Gretchen Whitmer fully funded pre-K, creating more competition for the district, Vitti added. The district also no longer recommends renovating Vetal, Vitti said, because the building is in worse condition than officials knew when the facilities plan was adopted and would cost far more to renovate. Under the proposal, the district would still retain $100 million in rainy day funds,Vitti said. Hannah Dellinger covers Detroit schools for Chalkbeat Detroit. You can reach her at hdellinger@chalkbeat.org. I’d live to see DPS schools and city libraries partner together on this one. School libraries are important to students. Having books on hand or easily accessible is key the key to improving literacy in Detroit. Your email address will not be published.
